phy_edx.6.0.summary: Your **mass** (how much matter you contain, in kg) is the same everywhere in the Universe, but your **weight** (the gravitational force on you, in N) depends on where you are. Weight is calculated with **W = m x g**, where g is the **gravitational field strength** of the planet, moon or star you are on. Because g depends mainly on the **mass of the body** (and its radius), an object weighs much less on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg) than on Earth (g = 10 N/kg) and much more on Jupiter, even though its mass never changes.

core.h: Mass and weight are different quantities
core.p: Students lose easy marks by mixing these up. **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object and is measured in **kilograms (kg)**. **Weight** is a **force**: the gravitational pull of a planet, moon or star on the object, measured in **newtons (N)**.
bullets: Mass is a **scalar**: it has size only.
Weight is a **vector**: it has size and direction, always **towards the centre** of the body doing the pulling.
Mass does **not** change when you move from Earth to the Moon or Mars.
Weight **does** change, because the strength of gravity is different on different bodies.
In everyday speech people say 'I weigh 60 kg'; in physics that is your mass, and your weight on Earth is 600 N.

callouts.p: Weight is the force acting on an object due to gravity. It is measured in newtons (N).

core.h: The weight equation: W = m x g
core.p: Edexcel gives this equation as one you must **recall and use**: weight (N) = mass (kg) x gravitational field strength (N/kg). It applies on any planet, moon or star; only the value of g changes.
bullets: **W = m x g**
W = weight in **newtons (N)**
m = mass in **kilograms (kg)**
g = gravitational field strength in **newtons per kilogram (N/kg)**
Rearranged: **m = W / g** and **g = W / m**
Convert grams to kilograms first: divide by 1000 (e.g. 250 g = 0.25 kg).

callouts.p: Use g = 10 N/kg on Earth unless the question gives a different value (Edexcel papers usually state g = 10 N/kg). The more precise value is about 9.8 N/kg.

core.p: A **gravitational field** is the region around a mass where another mass feels a force. The **gravitational field strength** tells you how many newtons of force act on each kilogram of mass placed in the field, which is why its unit is N/kg.
bullets: g = 10 N/kg means every 1 kg of mass feels a 10 N pull.
g has the same numerical value as the **acceleration of free fall** (10 m/s2 on Earth), ignoring air resistance.
Every object with mass has a gravitational field, but only very massive bodies (planets, moons, stars) have noticeable fields.
The field is strongest at the surface of the body and gets **weaker the further you are from it**.

callouts.p: The gravitational force acting on each kilogram of mass, g = W / m, measured in N/kg.

core.h: What decides the value of g on a planet or moon?
core.p: The spec asks you to **explain** why g, and therefore weight, differs on different bodies. The main reason is the **mass of the body**: the more mass a planet, moon or star has, the stronger its gravitational pull, so the larger g is at its surface.
bullets: **Greater mass of the planet = larger g = greater weight** for the same object.
**Distance from the centre** also matters: g is larger closer to the centre, so a dense, compact body can have a large surface g.
The Moon has about 1/80 of Earth's mass, so its surface g is much smaller (about 1/6 of Earth's).
Jupiter has over 300 times Earth's mass, so g at its cloud tops is about 2.5 times Earth's, even though Jupiter is much bigger in radius.
The Sun, with an enormous mass, has a surface g of roughly 270 N/kg.

callouts.p: Write: 'The Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth, so its gravitational field strength is smaller, so the same mass has a smaller weight.' Always link mass of body -> g -> weight.

core.h: Why you weigh less on the Moon
core.p: Take an 80 kg astronaut. On Earth W = 80 x 10 = 800 N. On the Moon W = 80 x 1.6 = 128 N. The astronaut has exactly the same amount of matter in both places, so the **mass is unchanged**, but the Moon pulls on each kilogram with a smaller force.
bullets: Mass on Earth = mass on Moon = 80 kg.
Weight on Moon is about **one sixth** of weight on Earth (1.6 / 10 = 0.16).
This is why Apollo astronauts could bound along and carry heavy backpacks easily.
Their **inertia** (resistance to changes in motion) was unchanged, so it was still hard to stop or turn quickly: that depends on mass, not weight.

core.p: You do not need to memorise every value, but you must be able to use any value given and explain the pattern. The values below are approximate surface values.

core.p: Weight is a force, so it is measured with a **newtonmeter** (a calibrated spring balance). Mass is found with a **balance** that compares the object with known masses, or is calculated from weight using m = W / g.
bullets: A newtonmeter stretches a spring: a smaller g on the Moon means less stretch, so a smaller reading.
A beam balance compares two masses; both are pulled equally weakly on the Moon, so it gives the **same reading** as on Earth.
Bathroom scales and kitchen scales actually measure force but are marked in kg assuming g = 10 N/kg, so they would read wrongly on the Moon.
Weight is directly proportional to mass: a graph of W against m is a straight line through the origin with **gradient = g**.

callouts.p: If a question plots weight (y-axis) against mass (x-axis) for a planet, the gradient of the line equals g for that planet.

core.h: Calculations: method that gets full marks
core.p: Weight questions are usually 2 or 3 marks. Mark schemes award a mark for the substitution and a mark for the correct answer with unit, so show every step.
bullets: 1. Write the equation: W = m x g.
2. Convert units (g to kg).
3. Substitute values with units.
4. Rearrange if needed (m = W / g, g = W / m).
5. Give the answer with the **correct unit** and sensible significant figures.
To compare two bodies, find the ratio of g values: weight ratio = g ratio (same mass).

callouts.p: Weight is never in kg. An answer of '128 kg' scores no answer mark, even if the number is right.

core.h: Falling and jumping on other bodies
core.p: Ignoring air resistance, any object falls with an acceleration equal to g. So objects fall more slowly on the Moon and faster on Jupiter. Since there is no atmosphere on the Moon, a hammer and a feather dropped together land at the same time.
bullets: Resultant force F = m x a; if weight is the only force, m x g = m x a, so **a = g**.
On the Moon, a = 1.6 m/s2: objects take longer to fall and you can jump higher.
All objects fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum, whatever their mass, because heavier objects have proportionally more weight but also more mass.
On Jupiter, a person would struggle to stand up because their weight would be about 2.5 times their Earth weight.

core.p: g is not the same everywhere around a planet: it is largest at the surface and gets smaller as you move further from the centre. This is why gravity is what keeps satellites and moons in orbit, and why astronauts far from Earth feel a smaller pull.
bullets: At the height of the International Space Station g is still about 9 N/kg: astronauts float because they are in **free fall**, not because there is no gravity.
Far out in space, between stars, g is extremely small, so weight is almost zero but mass is unchanged.
The pull of the Earth on the Moon and the Moon on the Earth are equal and opposite forces (Newton's third law).

callouts.p: Do not write 'there is no gravity in space'. Gravity acts over huge distances; it just gets weaker further away.

core.h: Linking to the rest of the topic
core.p: Gravity is the force behind the whole Astronomy topic. The same gravitational attraction that gives you weight keeps the planets orbiting the Sun and the Moon orbiting the Earth, and pulls clouds of gas and dust together to form stars.
bullets: Gravity provides the **centripetal force** for orbits (covered in 7.5P to 7.7P).
More massive bodies have stronger fields, so they dominate the motion of smaller ones.
Gravitational attraction causes a nebula to collapse and form a protostar (7.16P).

analogy.t: A bag of shopping and different strength magnets
analogy.p: Think of your mass as a bag holding a fixed number of iron balls. Each planet is like a magnet underneath you pulling on every ball. A massive planet such as Jupiter is a strong magnet pulling hard on each ball (large g), and the Moon is a weak magnet (small g). The number of balls (mass) never changes, but the total pull you feel (weight) depends on the magnet. Where it breaks down: gravity is not magnetism; it acts on all matter, is always attractive, and cannot be blocked or switched off.

terms.d: The amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg); it is the same everywhere.
The force acting on an object due to gravity, measured in newtons (N).
A region around a mass in which another mass experiences a force of attraction.
The gravitational force on each kilogram of mass, measured in N/kg; g = W / m.
The SI unit of force, including weight.
The unit of gravitational field strength.
A calibrated spring balance used to measure forces such as weight.
An instrument that measures mass, for example by comparing an object with known masses.
A quantity with size (magnitude) only, such as mass.
A quantity with size and direction, such as weight.
The acceleration of an object falling with only its weight acting on it; numerically equal to g.
The tendency of an object to resist changes in its motion; it depends on mass, not weight.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other; weight is directly proportional to mass for a fixed g.
A natural satellite that orbits a planet; Earth's Moon has a surface g of about 1.6 N/kg.

mistakes.w: Your mass is smaller on the Moon.
mistakes.r: Mass stays the same; only weight is smaller because g is smaller on the Moon.

mistakes.w: Weight is measured in kilograms.
mistakes.r: Weight is a force measured in newtons (N); mass is in kilograms (kg).

mistakes.w: There is no gravity on the Moon.
mistakes.r: The Moon has a gravitational field strength of about 1.6 N/kg, smaller than Earth's because the Moon has less mass.

mistakes.w: The Moon has lower gravity because it has no atmosphere.
mistakes.r: g depends on the mass (and radius) of the body, not on whether it has an atmosphere.

mistakes.w: g on the Moon is smaller because it is smaller in size.
mistakes.r: The key reason is that the Moon has a smaller mass than Earth, so its gravitational field is weaker.

mistakes.w: Using a mass in grams in W = m x g (e.g. 500 x 10 = 5000 N).
mistakes.r: Convert to kilograms first: 0.5 kg x 10 N/kg = 5 N.

mistakes.w: Astronauts in orbit are weightless because there is no gravity in space.
mistakes.r: Gravity still acts on them (g is about 9 N/kg at the ISS); they appear weightless because they are in free fall.

mistakes.w: g is the same on every planet.
mistakes.r: g is different on each body because each has a different mass and radius.

mistakes.w: Writing g = 10 N in the answer.
mistakes.r: Gravitational field strength has the unit N/kg; weight has the unit N.

exam.q: State the unit of gravitational field strength.
model: N/kg (newtons per kilogram)
exam.tip: m/s2 is also accepted on some mark schemes, but N/kg is the expected answer for field strength.

exam.q: State the equation linking weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
model: weight = mass x gravitational field strength (W = m x g)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols are both accepted; do not mix them up with F = m x a.

exam.q: An astronaut has a mass of 75 kg. Calculate her weight on the Moon. Gravitational field strength on the Moon = 1.6 N/kg.
exam.tip: Always include the unit N.

exam.q: A rock sample has a weight of 37 N on Mars, where g = 3.7 N/kg. Calculate the mass of the rock.
model: m = 10 kg
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting to avoid slips.

exam.q: The rock in the previous question is brought back to Earth. State its mass and calculate its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
model: Mass = 10 kg (unchanged)
Weight = 10 x 10 = 100 N
exam.tip: The examiner is checking you know mass does not change.

exam.q: Explain why an astronaut has a smaller weight on the Moon than on the Earth, even though her mass is the same.
model: The Moon has a smaller mass than the Earth
so the gravitational field strength on the Moon is smaller (1.6 N/kg compared with 10 N/kg)
weight = mass x g, so with the same mass the weight is smaller
exam.tip: Use the chain: mass of body -> g -> weight.

exam.q: A lander has a weight of 5000 N on Earth. Calculate its weight on Jupiter, where g = 25 N/kg (g on Earth = 10 N/kg).
model: weight on Jupiter = 500 x 25
exam.tip: Find the mass first, as it is the quantity that stays the same.

exam.q: A student measures the weight of different masses on Earth and plots weight against mass. Describe the graph and state what its gradient represents.
model: Straight line through the origin (weight directly proportional to mass)
Gradient = gravitational field strength (g)
exam.tip: 'Directly proportional' needs both a straight line and passing through the origin.

exam.q: A newtonmeter and a beam balance are both used to measure the same object on Earth and then on the Moon. Explain what happens to each reading.
model: Newtonmeter measures weight (force)
its reading falls on the Moon because g is smaller
Beam balance compares the object with known masses
both sides are affected equally by the smaller g, so its reading stays the same
exam.tip: Link each instrument to what it actually measures.

exam.q: Planet X has a gravitational field strength of 15 N/kg. Describe and explain how the weight of a 60 kg person, and the way objects fall, would differ on Planet X compared with Earth. Planet X is a different body with g = 15 N/kg; g on Earth = 10 N/kg.
model: Mass of the person stays 60 kg on both bodies
Weight on Earth = 60 x 10 = 600 N
Weight on Planet X = 60 x 15 = 900 N
Planet X probably has a greater mass (and/or smaller radius) giving a stronger gravitational field
Objects falling freely accelerate at g, so they accelerate at 15 m/s2 rather than 10 m/s2
so objects fall faster and the person could not jump as high / would find it harder to move about
exam.tip: 6-mark answers need calculations and explanations linked together; structure them in clear steps.

worked.q: A 250 g apple is taken to Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg). Calculate its weight on Mars and on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).
steps: Convert the mass: 250 g / 1000 = 0.25 kg
On Mars: W = m x g = 0.25 x 3.7 = 0.925 N
On Earth: W = 0.25 x 10 = 2.5 N
Mass stays 0.25 kg in both places.
worked.ans: About 0.93 N on Mars and 2.5 N on Earth.

worked.q: A space probe weighs 960 N on the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg). Find its weight on Earth (g = 10 N/kg).

phy_edx.6.1.summary: Our **Solar System** is made of the **Sun** (our star), **eight planets** and their **natural satellites** (moons such as our Moon), **dwarf planets** such as Pluto, and many **asteroids** and **comets**, all held in orbit by the Sun's gravity. You must know the planets in order from the Sun: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune**. Ideas about the Solar System have changed over time from the **geocentric** model (Earth at the centre) to the **heliocentric** model (Sun at the centre), because new technology such as the **telescope** produced new evidence, such as **Galileo's** discovery of moons orbiting Jupiter.

core.h: What is in our Solar System?
core.p: The Solar System is everything that is held in orbit by the Sun's gravity. Edexcel expects you to list its components using the right words.
bullets: **The Sun**: our star, which contains over 99% of the mass of the Solar System and gives out its own light.
**Eight planets**: large bodies that orbit the Sun.
**Natural satellites (moons)**: bodies that orbit planets, e.g. our Moon orbits the Earth.
**Dwarf planets**: smaller, roughly spherical bodies that orbit the Sun, e.g. Pluto and Ceres.
**Asteroids**: lumps of rock and metal orbiting the Sun, mostly in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
**Comets**: lumps of ice and dust that orbit the Sun in very elongated (elliptical) orbits.

callouts.p: The Sun is our star. It is the only object in the Solar System that is a source of light; planets and moons are seen because they reflect sunlight.

core.p: The Sun is a fairly average, main sequence star at the centre of the Solar System. Its enormous mass means its gravitational field dominates everything in the Solar System and keeps all the planets, dwarf planets, asteroids and comets in orbit around it.
bullets: It releases energy by **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen into helium in its core.
It is just one of billions of stars in our galaxy, the **Milky Way**.
The Solar System is therefore only a tiny part of the Milky Way galaxy, which is itself one of billions of galaxies in the Universe.

core.p: You must recall the **names and the order** of the planets, starting nearest the Sun. A mnemonic helps: **My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming** (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune).
bullets: 1 Mercury, 2 Venus, 3 Earth, 4 Mars: the **inner, rocky** (terrestrial) planets.
Then the **asteroid belt** between Mars and Jupiter.
5 Jupiter, 6 Saturn: the **gas giants**, the two largest planets.
7 Uranus, 8 Neptune: the outer **ice giants**.
Jupiter is the largest planet; Mercury is the smallest and closest to the Sun.
The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to complete one orbit (longer year).

callouts.p: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006, so there are eight planets, not nine.

core.p: The planets fall into two clear groups. Comparing them is a common short-answer question.
bullets: Inner planets are close to the Sun, so they are hotter and have short orbital periods.
Outer planets are far from the Sun, cold, and have long orbital periods (Neptune takes about 165 Earth years).
All the giant planets have many moons and ring systems; Saturn's rings are the most obvious.
Earth is the only planet known to support life and to have liquid water on its surface.

core.p: A **natural satellite** is a natural body that orbits a planet (or dwarf planet). Our Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. Mercury and Venus have no moons, while the giant planets have dozens.
bullets: Moons are kept in orbit by the **gravitational attraction of the planet** they orbit.
Jupiter's four largest moons are **Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto** (the Galilean moons).
Artificial satellites (e.g. the ISS, GPS satellites) are made by humans and are **not** part of the natural Solar System list.
Moons shine only by reflected sunlight.

callouts.p: A natural object that orbits a planet, for example the Moon orbits the Earth.

core.p: A **dwarf planet** orbits the Sun and is massive enough to be roughly spherical, but it has **not cleared other objects out of its orbit** and it is not a moon. This is what separates it from a full planet.
bullets: Examples: **Pluto**, **Ceres** (in the asteroid belt) and **Eris**.
Pluto was called the ninth planet from 1930 until 2006.
Astronomers then found other similar-sized bodies beyond Neptune, such as Eris, so the definition of a planet was tightened and Pluto became a dwarf planet.
This is an example of scientific ideas changing when new evidence appears.

core.p: Asteroids and comets are small bodies orbiting the Sun. They differ in what they are made of and in the shape of their orbits.
bullets: **Asteroids**: rocky and metallic, irregular in shape, most orbit in the **asteroid belt** between Mars and Jupiter in roughly circular orbits.
**Comets**: made of **ice and dust** (often called 'dirty snowballs').
Comets move in **highly elliptical** orbits, travelling from the far outer Solar System to close to the Sun.
Near the Sun the ice evaporates, forming a glowing coma and a **tail that points away from the Sun**.
Comets speed up as they get closer to the Sun and slow down as they move away (covered in the orbits notes).

core.p: Early astronomers, including the ancient Greeks such as Ptolemy (around AD 150), believed the **Earth was at the centre** of the Universe, with the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all orbiting the Earth in perfect circles. This is the **geocentric model**.
bullets: It was based on **naked-eye observations**: the Sun, Moon and stars appear to move across the sky around us each day.
We do not feel the Earth moving, so it seemed natural that the Earth was still.
It struggled to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backwards across the sky (retrograde motion); extra small circles (epicycles) were added to make it fit.
It was accepted for about 1500 years, partly because it fitted religious beliefs of the time.

callouts.p: A model of the Solar System in which the Earth is at the centre and the Sun, Moon, planets and stars orbit the Earth.

core.p: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published the **heliocentric model**: the **Sun is at the centre** and the Earth and other planets orbit the Sun in circular orbits. The Moon orbits the Earth.
bullets: It explained retrograde motion simply: Earth overtakes the slower outer planets as they all orbit the Sun.
It also explained the daily motion of the Sun and stars by the **Earth spinning on its axis**.
At first there was little direct evidence for it, and it went against accepted beliefs, so it was not widely accepted.
Later, Kepler showed that the orbits are in fact slightly elliptical rather than perfect circles.

callouts.p: A model of the Solar System in which the Sun is at the centre and the Earth and other planets orbit the Sun.

core.h: Galileo and the telescope: evidence for the heliocentric model
core.p: In 1610 Galileo Galilei used a newly invented **telescope** to observe the sky. He saw four 'stars' next to Jupiter that changed position from night to night. He concluded they were **moons orbiting Jupiter**.
bullets: This showed that **not everything orbits the Earth**, which contradicted the geocentric model.
Galileo also saw that **Venus shows a full set of phases** like the Moon, which is explained by Venus orbiting the Sun.
The telescope gave **new evidence** that naked-eye observers could not collect.
Galileo faced strong opposition from the Church, showing that new ideas are not always accepted straight away.

callouts.p: Models change when new technology (the telescope) produces new evidence (moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus) that the old model cannot explain.

core.h: The modern model and continuing change
core.p: Today's model has the Sun at the centre with the planets moving in **slightly elliptical, almost circular orbits**. The Sun is one star among billions in the Milky Way, so it is not the centre of the Universe.
bullets: Better telescopes discovered new planets: **Uranus (1781)** and **Neptune (1846)**.
Pluto was found in 1930 and reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 after more bodies were discovered.
Space probes and telescopes in space continue to add new moons, dwarf planets and comets.
This shows how science works: models are tested against evidence and **changed when evidence does not fit**.

analogy.t: A playground roundabout seen from the middle
analogy.p: If you sit in the middle of a spinning roundabout, everything in the playground seems to whirl around you, so you might think you are the centre of everything. That is the geocentric view: the sky seems to turn around us because the Earth is spinning. Only by gathering more evidence (like Galileo's telescope showing moons circling Jupiter) do you realise the playground is not moving around you. Where it breaks down: the roundabout spins about you, but the Earth also travels around the Sun once a year, and the planets have their own orbits at different speeds.

worked.q: Model answer: Why was the geocentric model accepted for so long, and why was it eventually rejected?
steps: Accepted: from Earth the Sun, Moon and stars appear to move around us; we cannot feel the Earth moving.

Rejected: Copernicus offered a simpler Sun-centred model explaining retrograde motion.
Galileo's telescope showed moons orbiting Jupiter and the phases of Venus, which the geocentric model could not explain.
worked.ans: It matched what people could see without instruments; it was replaced when telescope evidence showed bodies that did not orbit the Earth.

phy_edx.6.2.summary: Planets orbit the Sun, moons orbit planets, comets orbit the Sun and artificial satellites orbit the Earth, all because **gravity** provides a force directed towards the centre of the orbit. Planets and moons move in almost **circular** orbits, while comets have **highly elliptical** orbits and speed up near the Sun. In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so the **speed stays the same but the direction, and therefore the velocity, keeps changing**. For a stable orbit, **a change in speed requires a change in radius**: the closer the orbit, the faster the object must move.

core.p: An **orbit** is the curved path of one body around another, more massive body. It happens because the **gravitational force of attraction** pulls the smaller body towards the larger one, while the smaller body's motion carries it sideways. The result is a path that keeps curving around but never falls in.
bullets: Without gravity the body would travel in a **straight line** at constant speed (Newton's first law).
Gravity continually pulls it **towards the centre** of the orbit, bending its path into a circle or ellipse.
The force towards the centre needed to keep something moving in a circle is called the **centripetal force**; in orbits, **gravity provides the centripetal force**.
The more massive body sits at the centre of a circular orbit (or at one focus of an ellipse).

callouts.p: For every orbit in the Solar System, the centripetal force is provided by the gravitational attraction between the orbiting body and the body it orbits.

core.p: The eight planets orbit the **Sun**. Their orbits are **slightly elliptical but almost circular**, and they all go around in the same direction and roughly in the same plane.
bullets: The Sun's gravity provides the centripetal force.
Planets further from the Sun have **larger orbits**, move **more slowly** and so have **longer orbital periods** (longer years).
Mercury takes about 88 days; Earth 1 year; Neptune about 165 years.
In exam questions on circular motion, you can treat planetary orbits as circles.

core.p: **Moons** (natural satellites) orbit **planets** in near-circular orbits. The planet's gravity provides the centripetal force. Our Moon orbits the Earth about once every 27 days while the Earth-Moon pair orbits the Sun.
bullets: Many moons may orbit one planet; Jupiter and Saturn have dozens.
Moons closer to their planet orbit faster and have shorter periods than those further out, just like planets around the Sun.
Moons orbit planets; dwarf planets can also have moons (e.g. Pluto's moon Charon).

core.p: **Comets** orbit the **Sun** in **highly elliptical** (very stretched) orbits. They spend most of their time far out in the cold outer Solar System, then swing in close to the Sun before heading back out.
bullets: The Sun is **not at the centre** of the ellipse but close to one end (at a focus).
As a comet moves **towards the Sun**, gravity has a component along its direction of motion, so it **speeds up**: gravitational potential energy is transferred to kinetic energy.
It moves **fastest when closest to the Sun**, where the gravitational force is strongest.
As it moves away, gravity slows it down; it is **slowest when furthest from the Sun**.
Near the Sun ice evaporates and forms a tail that points **away from the Sun**.
Comet orbits are often tilted at large angles to the planets' orbits.

callouts.t: Only circular orbits have constant speed
callouts.p: Do not say a comet moves at a constant speed. Its distance from the Sun changes, so the gravitational force and its speed change around the orbit.

core.p: **Artificial satellites** are human-made objects put into orbit around the Earth (or other bodies). The Earth's gravity provides the centripetal force. They are used for communications, satellite navigation, weather forecasting, mapping, observing space and spying.
bullets: **Geostationary satellites** orbit **above the equator** at a large height (about 36 000 km) with a period of **24 hours**, in the same direction as Earth spins, so they stay above the same point on the surface. Used for **communications and satellite TV**: a dish can point at a fixed position.

**Polar orbit satellites** are much lower (a few hundred km), travel **over the North and South Poles** and orbit in about 90 to 100 minutes. The Earth rotates beneath them, so they can scan the whole surface: used for **weather monitoring, mapping and imaging**.
The **International Space Station** is in a low orbit, circling the Earth about every 90 minutes.

core.h: Speed and velocity: the key difference
core.p: To explain circular orbits you must use **speed** and **velocity** correctly. Speed is a **scalar** (how fast). Velocity is a **vector** (how fast and **in which direction**). So velocity can change even if speed does not, simply by changing direction.
bullets: Speed = distance / time; for a circular orbit, speed = 2 x pi x r / T (r = orbit radius, T = period).
Velocity changes if speed changes, **or direction changes, or both**.
**Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity, so an object changing direction is accelerating even at constant speed.
In an orbit the acceleration is **towards the centre**, in the same direction as the resultant force (gravity).

callouts.p: Speed in a given direction. It is a vector quantity.

core.h: Why speed stays constant but velocity changes in a circular orbit
core.p: This is the central explanation Edexcel asks for. In a circular orbit the gravitational force always acts **towards the centre**, which is **at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction of motion**.
bullets: Because the force is perpendicular to the motion, it has **no component along the direction of motion**, so it does not speed the object up or slow it down: **speed stays the same**.
The force does continually **change the direction** of motion, pulling the path round into a circle.
Since direction changes, **velocity changes** all the time.
A changing velocity means the object is **accelerating towards the centre** (centripetal acceleration).
Energy view: the distance from the centre stays the same, so gravitational potential energy does not change, and so kinetic energy (and speed) does not change.

callouts.p: Gravity acts towards the centre -> perpendicular to velocity -> changes direction, not speed -> velocity changes -> object accelerates towards the centre.

core.p: For a **stable orbit** there is only one speed that works at each distance. Closer to the central body, gravity is **stronger**, so the object must move **faster** to avoid being pulled in. Further away, gravity is **weaker**, so a **slower** speed is enough to stay in orbit.
bullets: **Smaller radius -> greater gravitational force -> higher orbital speed needed.**
**Larger radius -> weaker gravitational force -> lower orbital speed.**
So **if the orbital speed changes, the radius of the orbit must change** for the orbit to stay stable.
Larger orbits are also longer, so with a lower speed the **orbital period is much longer**.
This is why Mercury orbits fastest and Neptune slowest, and why low polar satellites move faster than geostationary ones.

callouts.p: For a stable orbit, if the speed of an orbiting object changes, the radius of its orbit must change: faster means a smaller orbit, slower means a larger orbit.

core.h: What happens if a satellite's speed changes?
core.p: Edexcel only needs a qualitative answer. If something changes the speed of an orbiting object, it cannot stay at the same radius.
bullets: If a satellite is **slowed down** (for example by drag from the thin upper atmosphere), gravity is now more than enough to hold it in that orbit, so it is pulled **closer** and moves to a **smaller radius**; eventually low satellites fall back and burn up.
If a satellite's rocket engines **speed it up**, gravity is not strong enough to keep it on the same path, so it moves **further out** to a **larger radius**.
If the object is too fast at a given distance it can escape; too slow and it falls inwards.
Engineers choose the launch speed to match the height of the orbit they want.

callouts.p: In a stable orbit a higher speed goes with a smaller radius. Do not write 'the faster it goes, the further out its orbit is' when comparing stable orbits.

core.h: Comparing the four types of orbit
core.p: A summary table helps for 'describe the orbits of...' questions.
bullets: All orbits are caused by gravity providing the centripetal force.
Only near-circular orbits have (nearly) constant speed.
The orbiting body is always less massive than the body at the centre.

head: Body
Orbits
Shape of orbit
Speed
rows: Fastest near the Sun, slowest far away

core.p: Top answers connect forces, energy and motion. Practise linking these ideas in longer explanations.
bullets: Newton's first law: without a resultant force the body would move in a straight line, so a resultant force (gravity) is needed for any orbit.
Newton's second law: the resultant force towards the centre gives an acceleration towards the centre.
Comet energy changes: as it falls in, GPE decreases and KE increases (speeds up); moving out, KE is transferred back to GPE (slows down).
The gravitational force gets weaker with distance, which links the shape of comet orbits to their changing speed.
Gravitational field strength depends on the mass of the central body: a more massive star would need its planets to orbit faster at the same distance.

analogy.t: Swinging a ball on a string
analogy.p: Whirl a ball on a string around your head at a steady rate. The string pulls the ball inwards towards your hand (like gravity pulling a planet towards the Sun), always at right angles to the ball's motion. The ball keeps the same speed but its direction changes all the time. Let go and it flies off in a straight line at a tangent, just as a planet would if gravity disappeared. Where it breaks down: the string's pull does not depend on distance, but gravity gets weaker further away, which is why outer planets move more slowly; and a string can only pull while it is taut, whereas gravity acts across empty space without contact.

terms.d: The curved path of a body around a more massive body, caused by gravitational attraction.
The resultant force directed towards the centre of a circle that keeps an object moving in a circular path.
The attractive force between any two masses; it provides the centripetal force for orbits.
Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar quantity.
Speed in a given direction; a vector quantity.
The rate of change of velocity; in a circular orbit it is directed towards the centre.
An orbit at a constant distance from the central body, travelled at constant speed.
An oval-shaped orbit in which the distance from the central body, and the speed, change.
The time taken to complete one full orbit.
The distance from the centre of the central body to the orbiting object.
An orbit in which the object stays at the same radius because its speed exactly matches the gravitational pull at that distance.
A natural body (moon) that orbits a planet.
A human-made object placed in orbit, for example for communications or weather monitoring.
A high orbit above the equator with a period of 24 hours, so the satellite stays above the same point on Earth.
A low orbit passing over the North and South Poles, so the Earth rotates beneath the satellite.
A body of ice and dust orbiting the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit.

mistakes.w: In a circular orbit the velocity is constant.
mistakes.r: The speed is constant but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes.

mistakes.w: The planet is not accelerating because its speed is constant.
mistakes.r: It is accelerating towards the centre because its velocity (direction) is changing.

mistakes.w: Gravity pushes the planet outwards / there is an outward force balancing gravity.
mistakes.r: The only force is gravity acting towards the centre; it provides the centripetal force, so the forces are not balanced.

mistakes.w: Gravity speeds the planet up in a circular orbit.
mistakes.r: Gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes direction but not speed.

mistakes.w: Comets move at a constant speed.
mistakes.r: Comets speed up as they approach the Sun and slow down as they move away, because their orbits are highly elliptical.

mistakes.w: Satellites further from Earth move faster.
mistakes.r: In a stable orbit, satellites further away move more slowly because gravity is weaker there.

mistakes.w: Comets orbit the Earth / planets.
mistakes.r: Comets orbit the Sun.

mistakes.w: Geostationary satellites do not move.
mistakes.r: They orbit the Earth once every 24 hours above the equator, so they only appear stationary from the ground.

mistakes.w: If a satellite slows down it moves to a higher orbit.
mistakes.r: If it slows down it moves closer, to a smaller radius; it would need to speed up to go to a higher orbit.

exam.q: Name the force that keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth.
model: Gravity / gravitational force (attraction) of the Earth
exam.tip: 'Centripetal force' alone may not score; say it is provided by gravity.

exam.q: State the shape of a comet's orbit.
model: (Highly) elliptical
exam.tip: 'Oval' is accepted on some schemes, but use 'elliptical'.

exam.q: State the direction of the resultant force on a planet in a circular orbit.
model: Towards the centre of the orbit / towards the Sun
exam.tip: Not 'downwards'.

exam.q: Describe the orbits of planets and comets.
model: Planets orbit the Sun in (almost) circular orbits
Comets orbit the Sun in highly elliptical orbits
exam.tip: Name what is being orbited as well as the shape.

exam.q: A satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at a constant speed. Explain why its velocity is changing.
model: Velocity is a vector / has direction
The direction of motion is constantly changing (so velocity changes even though speed is constant)
exam.tip: Mention direction explicitly.

exam.q: Explain how the speed of a comet changes as it moves around its orbit.
model: Speeds up as it approaches the Sun
because the gravitational force is stronger closer to the Sun / gravity acts partly along its direction of motion (GPE converted to KE)
fastest closest to the Sun and slowest furthest away
exam.tip: Link speed change to distance from the Sun.

exam.q: Satellite A is in a low orbit and satellite B is in a higher orbit around the Earth. Compare their orbital speeds and explain your answer.
model: Satellite A moves faster than B
A is closer so the gravitational force on it is stronger
so a greater speed is needed to stay in a stable orbit at a smaller radius
exam.tip: State the comparison, then the reason.

exam.q: Explain why a geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the Earth's surface.
model: It orbits above the equator
with a period of 24 hours / same time as the Earth takes to rotate once
in the same direction as the Earth rotates
exam.tip: Three separate conditions, three marks.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of forces, how a planet can have a changing velocity but a constant speed in a circular orbit.
model: Gravitational force from the Sun acts on the planet towards the centre
the force is perpendicular to the direction of motion / velocity
so it changes the direction of motion but not the speed
velocity is a vector, so changing direction means the velocity changes (the planet accelerates towards the centre)
exam.tip: Use 'perpendicular' or 'at right angles'; examiners look for it.

exam.q: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is slowed down by its thrusters. Explain what happens to the radius of its orbit.
model: The radius of the orbit decreases / it moves closer to the Earth
because at a lower speed gravity pulls it inwards; for a stable orbit a change in speed requires a change in radius
exam.tip: Qualitative only: no equations needed.

exam.q: Describe and explain the similarities and differences between the orbits of planets, moons, comets and artificial satellites.
model: All orbits are caused by gravity providing the centripetal force towards the central body
Planets orbit the Sun in almost circular orbits at almost constant speed
Moons orbit planets in almost circular orbits
Comets orbit the Sun in highly elliptical orbits, speeding up near the Sun and slowing far from it
Artificial satellites orbit the Earth, e.g. geostationary (24 h, high, above equator) or polar (low, fast, over poles)
Bodies in smaller orbits move faster and have shorter periods than those in larger orbits
exam.tip: Cover all four bodies and finish with a general rule linking radius and speed.

worked.q: The Earth orbits the Sun in a near-circular orbit of radius 150 000 000 km in 365 days. Calculate its orbital speed in km/s.
steps: Distance in one orbit = circumference = 2 x pi x r = 2 x 3.14 x 150 000 000 = 942 000 000 km
Speed = distance / time = 942 000 000 / 31 536 000
Speed = 29.9 km/s (about 30 km/s)
worked.ans: About 30 km/s. The speed is constant but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why the Moon accelerates even though it moves at a steady speed around the Earth.
steps: The Earth's gravitational force on the Moon acts towards the centre of the Earth.
This force is at right angles to the Moon's direction of motion.
So it changes the Moon's direction but not its speed.
Velocity is a vector, so a change in direction is a change in velocity; a changing velocity is an acceleration, directed towards the Earth.
worked.ans: The Moon accelerates towards the Earth because its velocity is constantly changing direction, even though its speed is constant.

worked.q: Applied example: Satellite P orbits at 400 km above the Earth, satellite Q at 36 000 km. Which has the longer period, and why?
steps: Q has a much larger orbit radius.
Gravity is weaker further from the Earth, so Q's stable orbital speed is lower.
Q also has to travel a much greater distance per orbit.
Lower speed and greater distance together give a much longer period (Q is geostationary: 24 hours; P takes about 90 minutes).
worked.ans: Q has the longer period, because it is further out, moves more slowly and travels further each orbit.

phy_edx.6.3.summary: Scientists have proposed two main models for the origin of the Universe. The **Steady State theory** says the Universe has always existed, is expanding, and new matter is continuously created so its density stays the same. The **Big Bang theory** says the Universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a very small, extremely hot and dense region and has been expanding and cooling ever since. Both theories explain the **red-shift** of galaxies, but only the Big Bang explains the **cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation**, so because there is more evidence supporting it, the Big Bang is the **currently accepted model**.

core.h: What is a model of the Universe?
core.p: A scientific model is an explanation that fits the observations we have. Models of the origin of the Universe try to answer: did the Universe have a beginning, and how has it changed over time? A model is only accepted while it agrees with the evidence; when new evidence is found that a model cannot explain, scientists replace or modify it.
bullets: Two models are named in the spec: the **Steady State theory** and the **Big Bang theory**.
Both were proposed in the 20th century once astronomers discovered that distant galaxies are **moving away** from us.
A good model must **explain existing observations** and **make predictions** that can be tested.
The model with **more supporting evidence** becomes the **currently accepted model**.
Models can change: the Steady State theory was popular for a while but was rejected when new evidence (the CMB) was discovered.

callouts.p: Scientists accept the theory that explains **all** of the evidence. If a theory cannot explain a reliable observation, it is rejected or changed.

core.p: The Steady State theory says the Universe has **no beginning and no end**. It has always existed and always will. It agrees that the Universe is **expanding**, but says that as galaxies move apart, **new matter is continuously being created** in the gaps between them. This new matter forms new galaxies, so the Universe looks the same on average at all times.
bullets: The Universe has **always existed** (it is infinitely old).
The Universe is **expanding**, so galaxies are moving apart.
**New matter is created continuously** as the Universe expands.
Because new matter fills the extra space, the **density of the Universe stays constant**.
On a large scale the Universe **looks the same at all times** (it is unchanging overall, which is why it is called steady state).
There was **no hot, dense early stage**, so the theory predicts **no leftover radiation** from the past.

callouts.p: The Universe has always existed and is expanding, with new matter being continuously created so that its density remains constant.

core.p: The Big Bang theory says the Universe **began at a single moment** about 13.8 billion years ago. All the matter and energy in the Universe was concentrated in a **very small, extremely hot and dense** region. Space itself then began to **expand**, and as it expanded the Universe **cooled**. Matter formed atoms, then stars and galaxies, which are still moving apart today.
bullets: The Universe **had a beginning**, so it has a **finite age** (about 13.8 billion years).
It started from a **very small, very hot, very dense** region.
The Universe has been **expanding ever since**, and it is still expanding today.
As it expanded, it **cooled down**.
**No new matter is created**: the same amount of matter spreads out over more space.
So the **density of the Universe decreases** over time.
The Big Bang is not an explosion into existing space: it is the **expansion of space itself**.

callouts.p: The Universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense, and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
Do not describe the Big Bang as a bomb exploding outwards from a centre. Space itself is expanding, carrying galaxies apart everywhere.

core.p: A compare question (spec 7.8P) always rewards at least one similarity. Both theories were built to explain the same key observation: galaxies are moving away from us, and the further away they are, the faster they are moving.
bullets: **Both** say the Universe is **expanding**.
**Both** say galaxies are **moving away** from each other (and from us).
**Both** can explain the **red-shift** of light from distant galaxies.
**Both** can explain why **more distant galaxies show a greater red-shift**.
**Both** are scientific theories based on observations and can be tested by evidence.

callouts.p: In a compare question give similarities AND differences, and always say what each theory says, for example: both say the Universe is expanding, but only the Steady State theory says new matter is being created.

core.p: The key differences are about the **beginning**, the **density** and whether **matter is created**. Learn the table: each row is a mark-scheme point.
bullets: Beginning: Big Bang says the Universe **had a beginning**; Steady State says it has **always existed**.
Matter: Steady State says **new matter is continuously created**; Big Bang says **no new matter** is created.
Density: Steady State says density is **constant**; Big Bang says density is **decreasing**.
Temperature: Big Bang says the Universe was once **extremely hot** and has **cooled**; Steady State has no hot early stage.
Change over time: Big Bang says the Universe **changes** (evolves); Steady State says it **looks the same** at all times.
CMB: Big Bang **predicts and explains** the CMB radiation; Steady State **cannot explain** it.

core.h: Evidence 1: red-shift of light from galaxies
core.p: When astronomers look at the spectrum of light from a distant galaxy, the dark absorption lines are in the same pattern as in a laboratory spectrum, but **shifted towards the red end** (to **longer wavelengths** and **lower frequencies**). This is **red-shift**. It means the galaxy is **moving away** from us. Light from **more distant galaxies is more red-shifted**, so more distant galaxies are moving away **faster**.
bullets: Red-shift is caused by the source **moving away** from the observer (the Doppler effect for light).
**Almost all** galaxies show red-shift, in **every direction** we look.
The **further away** a galaxy is, the **bigger its red-shift**, so the **faster** it is receding.
This pattern is best explained by the **whole Universe expanding**: space between galaxies is stretching.
Running the expansion **backwards** suggests that everything was once **close together** in a small region, which supports a Big Bang beginning.

callouts.p: The increase in wavelength (and decrease in frequency) of light from a galaxy moving away from us, so its spectral lines shift towards the red end of the spectrum.

core.p: Red-shift shows the Universe is expanding, and **both** theories include an expanding Universe. That is why red-shift on its own **cannot decide** between them. It supports both equally.
bullets: **Big Bang:** the Universe has been expanding since it began, so all galaxies are moving apart; galaxies that are further away are moving faster, so they show more red-shift.
**Steady State:** the Universe is also expanding (forever), so galaxies are moving apart and show red-shift; new matter fills the gaps so density stays constant.
So red-shift is **evidence for an expanding Universe**, and is **consistent with both** models.
Red-shift **supports the Big Bang** because tracing the expansion back in time points to a single starting point, but it does not rule out the Steady State theory.

callouts.p: Do not say red-shift disproves the Steady State theory. Both theories explain red-shift. It is the CMB that the Steady State theory cannot explain.

core.p: The **CMB radiation** is microwave radiation that is detected coming from **all directions** in space, with almost the **same intensity** everywhere. It was discovered by accident in 1965. The Big Bang theory explains it as the **leftover energy from the hot early Universe**. Radiation released when the Universe was very hot had a short wavelength; as the Universe expanded, this radiation was **stretched (red-shifted)** to much longer wavelengths, so today it is in the **microwave** region.
bullets: CMB comes from **every direction** in the sky, not from a particular star or galaxy.
It is **very uniform**: almost the same in every direction.
It is the **remnant (afterglow) of the Big Bang**, from when the Universe was very hot and dense.
The expansion of the Universe has **stretched** its wavelength, so it is now **microwave** radiation.
This corresponds to a very low temperature (about 2.7 K, just above absolute zero), showing the Universe has **cooled**.
The Big Bang theory **predicted** this radiation before it was found, which strongly supports the theory.

callouts.p: Microwave radiation received from all directions in space, which is the remnant of radiation from the hot, dense early Universe, stretched to longer wavelengths as the Universe expanded.

core.h: Why the Steady State theory cannot explain the CMB
core.p: The Steady State theory says the Universe has **always looked the same** and was **never hot and dense**. If there was never a hot, dense early stage, there would be no leftover radiation filling all of space. So the Steady State theory has **no explanation** for radiation that comes evenly from every direction.
bullets: Steady State: no beginning, so **no early hot phase**, so **no afterglow**.
Radiation from individual stars or galaxies would come from **particular points**, not uniformly from **all directions**.
The CMB was **predicted by the Big Bang** theory and **not by the Steady State** theory.
An observation that one theory predicts and the other cannot explain is powerful evidence for the first theory.

callouts.p: Red-shift: explained by BOTH theories. CMB: explained ONLY by the Big Bang theory.

core.h: Why the Big Bang is the currently accepted model
core.p: Spec point 7.10P: because there is **more evidence supporting the Big Bang theory** than the Steady State theory, the Big Bang is the **currently accepted model** for the origin of the Universe. The Big Bang explains **both** red-shift and the CMB; the Steady State explains only red-shift.
bullets: Big Bang explains **red-shift** (expansion) **and** the **CMB** (leftover radiation from the hot early Universe).
Steady State explains red-shift but **not** the CMB.
After the CMB was discovered in 1965, most scientists **abandoned the Steady State theory**.
The Big Bang is the accepted model because it is supported by **more evidence**, not because it is proven.
If new evidence appeared that the Big Bang could not explain, the model might have to be **changed** in the future.

callouts.p: As there is more evidence supporting the Big Bang theory than the Steady State theory, it is the currently accepted model for the origin of the Universe.
Never write that the Big Bang has been proven. Write that it is the currently accepted model because more evidence supports it.

core.p: Top-band answers link observation to explanation to conclusion in a logical chain. Practise saying it in order.
bullets: Observation: light from distant galaxies is **red-shifted**.
Explanation: so galaxies are **moving away**; more distant galaxies have **greater red-shift**, so are moving **faster**.
Conclusion: the **Universe is expanding**, which **both** theories include.
Observation: **CMB** microwave radiation is detected from **all directions**.
Explanation: Big Bang says it is **leftover radiation** from the **hot, dense early Universe**, **stretched** by expansion into microwaves.
Steady State has **no hot early stage**, so **cannot explain** the CMB.
Conclusion: **more evidence** supports the Big Bang, so it is the **currently accepted** model.

callouts.p: Use words like so, because and therefore to link each idea. Six mark questions reward a logically linked chain, not a list of facts.

core.p: This topic is a classic example of how scientific ideas develop. Scientists propose models, test their predictions, and keep the model that agrees best with the evidence. New technology (such as radio telescopes that detected the CMB) produces new evidence, which can cause a model to be rejected.
bullets: Two competing models can both fit the **existing** evidence for a time (both fitted red-shift).
A **new observation** (the CMB) can decide between them.
The successful theory made a **prediction** that was later **confirmed**.
Scientific knowledge is **tentative**: accepted models can be modified as new evidence is found.
Scientists share findings so others can **check and repeat** observations (peer review).

analogy.t: Baking a raisin loaf versus a magic self-refilling loaf
analogy.p: Big Bang: a raisin loaf rising in the oven. The dough (space) expands, every raisin (galaxy) moves away from every other raisin, and raisins further apart separate faster. The number of raisins stays the same, so they get more spread out (density falls), and the loaf started small and hot. Steady State: a magic loaf that rises forever but new raisins keep appearing in the gaps, so the loaf always looks equally crowded. Where it breaks down: a real loaf has an edge and a centre and expands into the oven, but the Universe has no centre and no edge, and space itself is what expands, not stuff moving through space.

terms.d: Everything that exists: all of space, time, matter and energy.
A huge collection of billions of stars held together by gravity.

The model in which the Universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
The idea that the space between galaxies is increasing, so galaxies are moving apart.
The mass of matter per unit volume of space; constant in the Steady State theory, decreasing in the Big Bang theory.
The Steady State idea that new matter is being created all the time to fill the space made by expansion.
The increase in wavelength and decrease in frequency of light from a source moving away from the observer, shifting spectral lines towards the red end.
A spectrum with dark lines at particular wavelengths, caused by elements absorbing light; the pattern acts like a fingerprint.
The change in observed frequency and wavelength of a wave when the source moves relative to the observer.
Cosmic microwave background radiation: microwave radiation from all directions in space, the remnant of radiation from the hot early Universe.
Part of the electromagnetic spectrum with longer wavelength than infrared and shorter than radio waves.
The model supported by the most evidence at present, which may change if new evidence is found.
Reliable observations or measurements that support or contradict a theory.
A testable statement of what a theory says should be observed; the Big Bang predicted the CMB.

mistakes.w: Red-shift proves the Big Bang theory and disproves Steady State.
mistakes.r: Red-shift shows the Universe is expanding and is explained by BOTH theories; only the CMB distinguishes them.

mistakes.w: The Steady State theory says the Universe is not expanding.
mistakes.r: The Steady State theory says the Universe IS expanding, with new matter created so density stays constant.

mistakes.w: The Big Bang was an explosion at the centre of the Universe.
mistakes.r: The Universe began from a very small, hot, dense region and space itself has been expanding everywhere; there is no centre.

mistakes.w: The Big Bang theory has been proven to be true.
mistakes.r: It is the currently accepted model because there is more evidence supporting it than the Steady State theory.

mistakes.w: The CMB comes from stars or from the Sun.
mistakes.r: The CMB comes from all directions and is leftover radiation from the hot early Universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths by expansion.

mistakes.w: In the Big Bang theory the density of the Universe stays the same.
mistakes.r: In the Big Bang theory no new matter is created, so as the Universe expands its density decreases.

mistakes.w: Red-shift means the galaxies are turning red.
mistakes.r: Red-shift means the wavelength of the light we receive increases, so spectral lines shift towards the red end of the spectrum.

mistakes.w: Both theories say the Universe had a beginning.
mistakes.r: Only the Big Bang says the Universe had a beginning; the Steady State says it has always existed.

exam.q: State one similarity between the Steady State theory and the Big Bang theory.
model: Both say the Universe is expanding (or both explain red-shift / galaxies moving apart).
exam.tip: Expanding is the safest similarity to give.

exam.q: Which theory of the Universe is the currently accepted model?
model: The Big Bang theory.
exam.tip: One word answers are fine for 1 mark state questions.

exam.q: According to the Steady State theory, the density of the Universe stays constant even though the Universe is expanding. Explain how this is possible.
model: New matter is (continuously) created
which fills the extra space, so mass per unit volume stays the same.
exam.tip: Link the creation of matter to the constant density.

exam.q: Describe the Big Bang theory of the origin of the Universe.
model: The Universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region
and has been expanding (and cooling) ever since.
exam.tip: Mention the starting state AND the expansion.

exam.q: Give two differences between the Steady State theory and the Big Bang theory.
model: Big Bang: Universe had a beginning; Steady State: it has always existed
Steady State: new matter is continuously created / density constant; Big Bang: no new matter / density decreases.
exam.tip: Each difference must say what BOTH theories claim.

exam.q: Explain why the red-shift of galaxies does not allow scientists to decide between the Big Bang and Steady State theories.
model: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving away / the Universe is expanding
both theories say the Universe is expanding, so both explain red-shift.
exam.tip: The key word is both.

exam.q: What is the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation and how does the Big Bang theory explain it?
model: Microwave radiation detected from all directions in space
it is leftover (remnant) radiation from when the Universe was very hot and dense
expansion of the Universe stretched its wavelength into the microwave region.
exam.tip: Say where it comes from AND why it is now microwaves.

exam.q: Explain why the discovery of the CMB radiation led scientists to reject the Steady State theory.
model: The CMB is explained as radiation left over from a hot, dense early Universe
the Steady State theory says the Universe has always been the same / was never hot and dense
so the Steady State theory cannot explain the CMB (but the Big Bang can / predicted it).
exam.tip: Contrast what each theory says about the early Universe.

exam.q: Explain why the Big Bang theory, rather than the Steady State theory, is the currently accepted model of the Universe.
model: Red-shift shows the Universe is expanding
both theories can explain red-shift
the CMB can only be explained by the Big Bang theory (leftover radiation from hot early Universe)
so there is more evidence supporting the Big Bang theory.
exam.tip: Structure: evidence 1, both explain it; evidence 2, only Big Bang explains it; conclusion.

exam.q: Compare the Steady State theory and the Big Bang theory, and explain how the evidence from red-shift and CMB radiation supports each theory.
model: Both theories say the Universe is expanding
Big Bang: Universe began from a small, hot, dense region / has a finite age; Steady State: always existed / no beginning
Steady State: new matter continuously created so density constant; Big Bang: no new matter so density decreases
Red-shift: light from distant galaxies shifted to longer wavelengths, more distant galaxies more red-shifted, so Universe expanding
red-shift is explained by both theories
CMB: microwave radiation from all directions, remnant of hot early Universe stretched by expansion
only the Big Bang explains the CMB, so it has more supporting evidence and is the accepted model.
exam.tip: Level 3 answers cover similarities, differences AND both pieces of evidence, linked to a conclusion.

worked.q: A student writes: 'Galaxies are red-shifted, so the Steady State theory must be wrong.' Explain what is wrong with this statement and correct it.
steps: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving away from us, so the Universe is expanding.
The Steady State theory also says the Universe is expanding (with new matter being created).
So red-shift is consistent with the Steady State theory as well as the Big Bang theory.
The evidence that the Steady State theory cannot explain is the CMB radiation.
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: red-shift supports both theories. The Steady State theory is rejected because it cannot explain the CMB radiation, which the Big Bang theory explains as leftover radiation from the hot early Universe.

worked.q: Model answer: compare what the two theories say about how the Universe will look in 10 billion years' time.
steps: Steady State: the Universe is unchanging overall; new matter keeps forming new galaxies.
So in 10 billion years the density and overall appearance would be the same as today.
Big Bang: the Universe keeps expanding and no new matter is created.
So galaxies would be further apart, the density lower and the Universe cooler than today.
worked.ans: Steady State predicts the Universe would look the same with the same density; the Big Bang predicts galaxies further apart, lower density and lower temperature.

worked.q: Applied example: in 1965 two radio engineers detected a faint microwave signal that was the same in every direction they pointed their antenna. Explain why this was important.
steps: Radiation coming equally from every direction cannot come from a single star or galaxy.
The Big Bang theory predicted that radiation left from the hot, dense early Universe should fill all of space.
Expansion would have stretched this radiation to long wavelengths, into the microwave region.
The Steady State theory has no hot early stage, so predicts no such radiation.
worked.ans: They had discovered the CMB radiation. Only the Big Bang theory could explain it, so it provided the extra evidence that made the Big Bang the currently accepted model.

phy_edx.6.4.summary: When a wave source moves relative to an observer, the observed **frequency and wavelength change**: this is the **Doppler effect**. Light from distant galaxies is **red-shifted** (shifted to longer wavelengths), and the **further away** a galaxy is, the **greater its red-shift**, which shows that galaxies are moving away and the **Universe is expanding**. Both the Big Bang and Steady State theories explain red-shift, but the discovery of the **cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation**, which only the Big Bang can explain, led to the Big Bang becoming the **currently accepted model**.

core.p: If a wave source is **moving relative to an observer**, there will be a **change in the observed frequency and wavelength**. You hear this with sound: an ambulance siren sounds **higher pitched** as it approaches you and **lower pitched** as it moves away. The source itself is not changing its sound; the motion changes the waves that reach you.
bullets: Source moving **towards** the observer: observed wavelength **decreases**, observed frequency **increases**.
Source moving **away from** the observer: observed wavelength **increases**, observed frequency **decreases**.
The **faster** the source moves, the **bigger** the change in frequency and wavelength.
The **speed of the wave does not change**: it depends on the medium (or, for light, is always the speed of light).
Because wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda) and v is fixed, if the wavelength goes up the frequency must go down.
The Doppler effect happens for **all waves**: sound, water waves and **electromagnetic waves including light**.

callouts.p: If a wave source is moving relative to an observer there will be a change in the observed frequency and wavelength.
Never write that the wave speeds up or slows down. Only the observed frequency and wavelength change.

core.p: A source sends out wavefronts at a steady rate. If the source moves, each new wavefront is emitted from a **slightly different place**. In front of the source the wavefronts are **squashed together**; behind it they are **spread out**. The observer counts how many wavefronts arrive each second (frequency) and how far apart they are (wavelength).
bullets: In front of a moving source: wavefronts closer together, so **shorter wavelength** and **higher frequency**.
Behind a moving source: wavefronts further apart, so **longer wavelength** and **lower frequency**.
An observer at the side, or a stationary source, sees no change.
The source's own (emitted) frequency has not changed; only what the observer **detects** is different.

callouts.p: If asked to explain using a wavefront diagram, say the waves are bunched together (shorter wavelength) on one side and spread out (longer wavelength) on the other, then link to frequency.

core.h: The Doppler effect for light: red-shift and blue-shift
core.p: Light is a wave, so it shows the Doppler effect too. In the visible spectrum, **red** light has the **longest wavelength** and **violet** the shortest. So if a light source moves away, its light shifts towards the red end: **red-shift**. If it moves towards us, its light shifts towards the blue/violet end: **blue-shift**.
bullets: **Red-shift**: source moving **away**; observed wavelength **longer**, frequency **lower**.
**Blue-shift**: source moving **towards** us; observed wavelength **shorter**, frequency **higher**.
The **bigger the shift**, the **faster** the source is moving relative to us.
Almost all galaxies are **red-shifted**; only a few very close galaxies (such as Andromeda) are blue-shifted.
The object does not look red: the shift is measured from the positions of **spectral lines**.

callouts.p: The increase in the observed wavelength (and decrease in frequency) of light from a source moving away from the observer, so spectral lines shift towards the red end of the spectrum.

core.h: How astronomers measure red-shift: absorption lines
core.p: Elements in a star's outer layers absorb light at particular wavelengths, producing **dark absorption lines** in its spectrum. Each element has its own unique pattern of lines, like a barcode. Scientists compare the pattern from a galaxy with the same pattern measured in a **laboratory**. If the whole pattern is moved to longer wavelengths, the light is red-shifted.
bullets: The **pattern** (spacing) of lines stays the same, so we can recognise the element.
The **position** of the pattern moves: towards red for red-shift.
The **size of the shift** tells us how fast the galaxy is moving away.
Comparing with a **stationary lab source** is essential: it gives the unshifted reference wavelengths.

callouts.p: Red-shift is seen as a known pattern of spectral lines shifted towards longer wavelengths compared with a source on Earth.

core.h: Red-shift of galaxies at different distances (7.12P)
core.p: Edwin Hubble and others measured the red-shift of many galaxies and their distances. They found that **light from more distant galaxies is more red-shifted**. Since a bigger red-shift means a faster speed away from us, **the further away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away**.
bullets: Nearby galaxies: **small** red-shift, moving away **slowly**.
Distant galaxies: **large** red-shift, moving away **quickly**.
Red-shift **increases with distance**: speed of recession is roughly **proportional** to distance.
Red-shift is seen in galaxies in **every direction**, not just one part of the sky.
The light from the most distant galaxies left them billions of years ago.

callouts.p: For full marks say BOTH: light from galaxies is red-shifted AND the further away the galaxy, the greater the red-shift.

core.p: If you plot the speed at which galaxies are moving away (worked out from red-shift) against their distance from Earth, you get a **straight line through the origin**. This means speed is **directly proportional** to distance: a galaxy twice as far away is moving away about twice as fast.
bullets: Straight line through origin: **speed proportional to distance**.
This is exactly what you would expect if **space itself is stretching** uniformly.
In an expanding Universe, **every** galaxy sees almost every other galaxy moving away from it, so there is **no centre**.
More space between two galaxies means more stretching, so they separate **faster**.

core.h: Why red-shift is evidence for an expanding Universe (7.13P)
core.p: If galaxies in **every direction** are moving away from us, and the **more distant ones are moving faster**, the simplest explanation is that the **space between all galaxies is expanding**. Think of dots on a balloon being blown up: every dot moves away from every other dot, and dots further apart separate faster.
bullets: Red-shift shows galaxies are **moving away** from us.
Red-shift is seen in **all directions**, so it is not just one group of galaxies moving.
**Greater red-shift for more distant galaxies** means speed increases with distance.
This pattern means the **whole Universe is expanding**.
Running the expansion **backwards in time**, the galaxies would have been **closer together**, suggesting the Universe started from a very small region.

callouts.p: Red-shift, so galaxies moving away. More distant, more red-shift, so faster. Therefore the Universe is expanding.
Every galaxy would observe the same pattern, so red-shift does not mean the Earth is at the centre of the Universe.

core.h: How the Big Bang theory accounts for red-shift (7.14P)
core.p: The Big Bang theory says the Universe began from a **very small, extremely hot and dense region** and has been **expanding ever since**. Because space is expanding, galaxies are carried apart, so their light is red-shifted. Galaxies further away have more expanding space between us and them, so they move away faster and show **greater red-shift**.
bullets: Universe expanding since it began, so galaxies **move apart**, so light is **red-shifted**.
Further galaxies recede **faster**, so **greater red-shift**: matches observations.
Tracing back the expansion leads to a **single starting point**, consistent with a beginning.
In the Big Bang no new matter is created, so the Universe's **density decreases** as it expands.

core.h: How the Steady State theory accounts for red-shift (7.14P)
core.p: The Steady State theory **also** says the Universe is **expanding**, so it also predicts that galaxies move apart and their light is red-shifted, with more distant galaxies moving away faster. The difference is that it says the Universe has **always existed**, and **new matter is continuously created** in the gaps so that the **density stays constant**.
bullets: Universe always expanding, so galaxies **move apart**, so light is **red-shifted**.
More distant galaxies recede faster, so **greater red-shift**: also matches observations.
New matter forms new galaxies in the space created, so the Universe **looks the same** at all times.
So **red-shift alone cannot decide** between the two theories.

callouts.p: A very common wrong answer is that the Steady State theory cannot explain red-shift. It can, because it includes expansion.

core.p: The **CMB radiation** is **microwave** radiation that reaches Earth from **all directions** in space with almost the **same intensity**. The Big Bang theory explains it as the **leftover radiation from the hot, dense early Universe**. When it was released it had a much shorter wavelength, but the **expansion of the Universe has stretched** it (it has been red-shifted) into the **microwave** part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
bullets: Detected from **every direction**, not from individual stars or galaxies.
Almost **uniform** across the whole sky.
It is the **remnant (afterglow)** of radiation from soon after the Big Bang.
As the Universe **expanded and cooled**, the wavelength of this radiation **increased**.
It now corresponds to a temperature of about 2.7 K, just above absolute zero.
It was **discovered in 1965** using a radio antenna, after being **predicted** by the Big Bang theory.

callouts.p: Microwave radiation coming from all directions in space, which is the remnant of radiation from the hot, dense early Universe, stretched to microwave wavelengths by the expansion of the Universe.
