core.h: How the CMB led to the Big Bang being accepted (7.15P)
core.p: Before 1965, both theories explained red-shift, so scientists could not choose between them. The Big Bang theory **predicted** that radiation from the hot early Universe should still fill space, stretched to long wavelengths. When the **CMB was discovered**, it matched this prediction. The Steady State theory says the Universe was **never hot and dense**, so it **cannot explain** the CMB. So the Big Bang became the **currently accepted model**.
bullets: Red-shift: explained by **both** theories, so not decisive.
CMB: **predicted** by the Big Bang, **explained only** by the Big Bang.
Steady State has **no hot, dense early stage**, so predicts **no background radiation**.
Radiation from stars and galaxies would come from **particular points**, not evenly from all directions.
There is now **more evidence** for the Big Bang than for Steady State, so it is the **currently accepted model**.
It is accepted, **not proven**: it could be modified if new evidence is found.

callouts.p: The CMB is the evidence that the Big Bang explains and the Steady State theory cannot, so its discovery led to the Big Bang becoming the accepted model.

core.p: Six mark questions on this point usually ask you to explain how evidence supports a theory. Build a chain from wave physics to cosmology.
bullets: Doppler effect: moving source, so **change in observed wavelength and frequency**.
Light from galaxies: lines shifted to **longer wavelength** (red-shift), so galaxies are **moving away**.
**More distant galaxies, greater red-shift**, so faster, so **Universe expanding**.
Both Big Bang and Steady State include expansion, so **both explain red-shift**.
CMB: **microwaves from all directions**, leftover from **hot, dense early Universe**, **stretched** by expansion.
Only the Big Bang explains CMB, so **more evidence** for it, so it is the **accepted model**.

callouts.p: Longer wavelength, lower frequency, moving away, more distant, greater red-shift, expanding, all directions, microwave, leftover radiation, more evidence.

analogy.t: The ants on a balloon and the passing siren
analogy.p: Draw dots (galaxies) on a balloon and blow it up. Every dot moves away from every other dot, and dots that start further apart separate faster, exactly like the red-shift and distance pattern; no dot is at the centre. Now draw a wiggly wave on the balloon: as it inflates the wave is stretched to a longer wavelength, like the CMB being stretched into microwaves. A passing ambulance siren shows the Doppler effect: higher pitch coming towards you, lower going away. Where it breaks down: the balloon's surface is 2D and expands into the room around it, but the Universe is not expanding into anything; and the siren's Doppler shift is caused by the source moving through air, while cosmological red-shift is caused by space itself stretching.

terms.d: The change in observed frequency and wavelength of a wave when the source is moving relative to the observer.
The number of waves reaching the observer per second, which can differ from the frequency emitted by a moving source.
The distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave, measured in metres.
Increase in observed wavelength and decrease in frequency of light from a source moving away, shifting spectral lines towards the red end.
Decrease in observed wavelength and increase in frequency of light from a source moving towards the observer.
The range of wavelengths (colours) of light from a source, spread out from violet to red.
Dark lines in a spectrum at particular wavelengths where elements have absorbed light; each element has a unique pattern.
A huge group of billions of stars held together by gravity.
The movement of a galaxy away from us.
The idea that space between galaxies is stretching, so galaxies are moving apart and more distant ones recede faster.
The Universe began from a very small, extremely hot and dense region and has been expanding and cooling ever since.
The Universe has always existed and is expanding, with new matter continuously created so density stays constant.
Cosmic microwave background radiation: microwaves from all directions, the remnant of radiation from the hot early Universe stretched by expansion.
Electromagnetic waves with wavelengths longer than infrared and shorter than radio waves.
The model supported by most evidence at present; the Big Bang theory, because it explains both red-shift and the CMB.
wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x lambda); with v fixed, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.

model: When a wave source moves relative to an observer
there is a change in the observed frequency and wavelength.

model: Red-shift shows galaxies are moving away from us
seen in (almost) all directions / for almost all galaxies
more distant galaxies have greater red-shift so are moving faster, so space is expanding.
exam.tip: A full chain: red-shift, moving away, all directions, further faster, expanding.

exam.q: Explain how both the Big Bang theory and the Steady State theory account for the red-shift of galaxies.

so galaxies are moving apart and light is red-shifted
Steady State: Universe has always been expanding (with new matter created)
so galaxies are also moving apart and light is red-shifted.

the Steady State theory says the Universe was never hot and dense so cannot explain the CMB
so there is more evidence for the Big Bang (both explain red-shift but only Big Bang explains CMB).

exam.q: The spectrum of light from galaxy X has an absorption line at 670 nm. The same line from a lab source is at 656 nm. Galaxy Y shows the same line at 700 nm. State and explain which galaxy is further from Earth.
model: Both lines are at a longer wavelength than the lab value, so both galaxies are red-shifted / moving away
galaxy Y has the greater red-shift (44 nm compared with 14 nm)
so galaxy Y is moving away faster and is further away.

model: Light from distant galaxies is red-shifted: longer wavelength, lower frequency (Doppler effect)
so galaxies are moving away; more distant galaxies have greater red-shift so move faster
so the Universe is expanding
both theories include expansion so both explain red-shift
CMB: microwave radiation from all directions, remnant of the hot, dense early Universe stretched by expansion
the Steady State theory has no hot dense beginning so cannot explain the CMB
so more evidence supports the Big Bang, the currently accepted model.
exam.tip: Level 3 answers link the Doppler effect, red-shift, expansion and the CMB in a logical chain with a clear conclusion.

worked.q: A lab measures a hydrogen absorption line at 656 nm. In light from galaxy P the line is at 663 nm; from galaxy Q it is at 690 nm. Compare the two galaxies.
steps: Shift for P = 663 - 656 = 7 nm towards longer wavelength.
Shift for Q = 690 - 656 = 34 nm towards longer wavelength.
Both shifts are to longer wavelength, so both galaxies are red-shifted and moving away.
Q has the larger red-shift, so Q is moving away faster.
Because more distant galaxies have greater red-shift, Q is further away than P.
worked.ans: Both galaxies are moving away from us; galaxy Q (34 nm shift) is moving away faster and is further away than galaxy P (7 nm shift).

worked.q: A sound source emits waves of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m/s. Explain, using v = f x lambda, what a listener detects as the source moves towards them.
steps: Emitted wavelength = v / f = 340 / 500 = 0.68 m.
As the source moves towards the listener, wavefronts are bunched together in front of it.
So the observed wavelength is less than 0.68 m.
The speed of sound in air is still 340 m/s.
Since f = v / lambda and lambda is smaller, the observed frequency is greater than 500 Hz.
worked.ans: The listener detects a shorter wavelength (less than 0.68 m) and a higher frequency (more than 500 Hz), so a higher pitch; the wave speed is unchanged.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why the CMB is now detected as microwaves even though it was released when the Universe was extremely hot.
steps: Radiation released by the hot early Universe had a short wavelength and high energy.
Since then the Universe has expanded enormously.
The expansion of space has stretched the wavelength of this radiation (it has been red-shifted).
Its wavelength has increased into the microwave region, matching a very cold temperature of about 2.7 K.
worked.ans: Expansion of the Universe has stretched the radiation's wavelength from short wavelengths to the much longer microwave wavelengths, showing the Universe has expanded and cooled.

phy_edx.6.5.summary: Every star forms from a **nebula** (a cloud of dust and gas) pulled together by **gravity**, and then spends most of its life as a stable **main sequence star**, fusing hydrogen into helium. A star of **similar mass to the Sun** then becomes a **red giant** and finally a **white dwarf**, while a star **much more massive than the Sun** becomes a **red supergiant**, explodes as a **supernova** and leaves a **neutron star** or a **black hole**. Every stage is controlled by the **balance between thermal expansion** (outward pressure from the energy released by fusion) **and gravity** (pulling inwards): when the two are balanced the star is stable; when one wins, the star expands or collapses.

core.h: Overview: mass decides a star's fate
core.p: All stars begin the same way, in a nebula, and all spend a long stable phase on the main sequence. What happens afterwards depends on the star's **mass**. More mass means **stronger gravity**, so the core becomes hotter and denser, fusion is faster, and the star's life is **shorter and more violent**.
bullets: Stars of **similar mass to the Sun**: nebula, main sequence star, red giant, white dwarf.
Stars with **mass much larger than the Sun**: nebula, main sequence star, red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole.
The key idea linking every stage is the **balance between thermal expansion and gravity**.
**Nuclear fusion** in the core releases the energy that keeps a star shining and hot.

callouts.p: Sun-like: red giant then white dwarf. Massive: red supergiant then supernova then neutron star or black hole.

core.p: A star begins as a **nebula**, a huge cloud of **dust and gas** (mainly **hydrogen**) in space. **Gravity** pulls the particles together, so the cloud **collapses** and becomes denser. As it collapses, gravitational potential energy is transferred to the particles' kinetic energy, so the gas **heats up**. The hot, dense ball forming at the centre is sometimes called a **protostar**.
bullets: Nebula = cloud of **dust and gas**, mostly hydrogen.
**Gravity** pulls the material together and it **collapses**.
The material gets **denser** and **hotter** as it collapses.
When the core is **hot enough and dense enough**, **nuclear fusion** of hydrogen nuclei begins.
Once fusion starts, the star is born and joins the **main sequence**.

callouts.p: A cloud of dust and gas (mainly hydrogen) in space, from which stars form when gravity pulls the material together.

core.p: In a **main sequence star**, **hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei** in the core, releasing huge amounts of energy. This is the **longest and most stable** stage of a star's life. The Sun is a main sequence star and has been for about 4.6 billion years.
bullets: Fuel: **hydrogen** in the core; product: **helium**.
Fusion releases energy, which keeps the core **very hot**.
The star is **stable**: it does not expand or contract, because the **outward force from thermal expansion balances the inward force of gravity**.
This stage lasts **billions of years** for a star like the Sun.
**More massive** stars use up their hydrogen **faster**, so their main sequence stage is **shorter**, even though they have more fuel.

callouts.p: A stable star in which hydrogen nuclei are fusing to form helium in the core, with the outward pressure from thermal expansion balancing the inward pull of gravity.

core.h: The balance between thermal expansion and gravity (7.17P)
core.p: Two effects act on a star all the time. **Gravity** pulls all the star's matter **inwards**, trying to make it collapse. The energy released by **fusion** heats the gas, and hot gas tends to **expand**, pushing **outwards** (thermal expansion, which acts as an outward pressure). The size and stability of the star depend on which effect is bigger.
bullets: **Gravity = thermal expansion**: forces balanced, star is **stable** (main sequence).
**Thermal expansion > gravity**: the star **expands** (for example, becoming a red giant or red supergiant).
**Gravity > thermal expansion**: the star (or its core) **contracts or collapses** (for example, at the start of a white dwarf or supernova).
When fusion **slows or stops**, less energy is released, so the outward pressure falls and **gravity makes the core contract**.
Contraction makes the core **hotter**, which can start **new fusion reactions** of heavier elements, so the star can expand again.
More mass means **stronger gravity**, so a higher temperature is needed to balance it, so fusion is **faster**.

callouts.p: A star is stable when the outward force from thermal expansion (caused by energy from fusion) balances the inward force of gravity.
Do not say the star is held up by air pressure or magnetism. The outward effect is thermal expansion (gas pressure) caused by energy released by fusion.

core.p: When a star like the Sun has **used up the hydrogen in its core**, fusion there slows, so the outward pressure falls and **gravity makes the core contract**. The core gets **hotter**, and fusion of **helium into heavier elements** (such as carbon) begins, while hydrogen fuses in a shell around the core. The extra energy makes the **outer layers expand** enormously. As they expand they **cool**, so the star glows **red**: it is a **red giant**.
bullets: Trigger: **hydrogen in the core runs out**.
Gravity wins briefly: **core contracts and heats up**.
**Helium fuses** to form heavier elements such as **carbon**.
**Outer layers expand** hugely: thermal expansion now beats gravity in the outer layers.
The surface **cools**, so it looks **red**, but the star is much **larger and brighter** overall.
The Sun is expected to become a red giant in about 5 billion years.

callouts.p: A large star with a cool red surface, formed when a star of similar mass to the Sun runs out of hydrogen in its core and its outer layers expand.
A red giant's surface is cooler than the Sun's surface, but its core is hotter. Red does not mean hotter.

core.p: Eventually the red giant **runs out of fuel** it can fuse. The **outer layers drift away** into space as a shell of gas. With no fusion, there is no outward thermal expansion to balance gravity, so the remaining **core collapses** under gravity into a **white dwarf**: a **small, very dense, very hot** object about the size of the Earth.
bullets: **Fusion stops**, so outward pressure is lost.
**Outer layers are lost** into space (they can form a glowing shell of gas).
**Gravity** squeezes the leftover core into a tiny, **extremely dense** star.
A white dwarf is **hot**, so it glows white, but it is **dim** because it is so small.
No fusion happens, so it **slowly cools down** over a very long time (eventually it would become a cold, dark black dwarf).
This is the end of the Sun's life cycle: the Sun will **not** become a supernova or black hole because it does not have enough mass.

callouts.p: The small, hot, very dense core left behind when a star of similar mass to the Sun has lost its outer layers; no fusion occurs and it gradually cools.

core.h: Stars much more massive than the Sun (7.18P)
core.p: A star with a mass **much larger than the Sun** forms in the same way (nebula to main sequence) but has **stronger gravity**, so its core is **hotter and denser** and it fuses hydrogen much **faster**. Its main sequence life is therefore **shorter**. When core hydrogen runs out, it swells into a **red supergiant**, much bigger than a red giant.
bullets: Same start: **nebula** then **main sequence star**.
Stronger gravity, so higher core temperature, so **faster fusion**, so **shorter life**.
Hydrogen runs out: core contracts and heats, outer layers expand: **red supergiant**.
In a red supergiant, **successive fusion reactions** make heavier and heavier elements in the core, up to **iron**.
Fusing iron does **not** release energy, so once the core is iron, fusion stops.

callouts.p: A very large, cool-surfaced red star formed when a star much more massive than the Sun runs out of hydrogen in its core and its outer layers expand.

core.p: When the core of a red supergiant can no longer release energy by fusion, there is **no outward thermal expansion** to balance its enormous gravity. The core **collapses suddenly**, and the outer layers are blasted away in a gigantic explosion called a **supernova**. For a short time a supernova can be brighter than a whole galaxy.
bullets: Fusion stops, so **gravity wins**: core collapses in a fraction of a second.
The collapse causes a huge **explosion**: the **supernova**.
Elements **heavier than iron** are made in the extreme conditions of the explosion.
The supernova **spreads elements** (including heavy ones) out into space.
This material can form new **nebulae**, from which new stars and planets form; the elements in the Earth and our bodies were made in stars.

callouts.p: The huge explosion of a massive star (red supergiant) when its core collapses at the end of its life, throwing its outer layers into space.

core.h: After a supernova: neutron star or black hole
core.p: The supernova leaves behind the collapsed core. What it becomes depends on how much mass remains. If the remaining core is very dense but not too massive it becomes a **neutron star**. If the star was **extremely massive**, gravity is so strong that the core keeps collapsing into a **black hole**.
bullets: **Neutron star**: an extremely **dense** object made mostly of **neutrons**, only a few kilometres to tens of kilometres across.
**Black hole**: forms from the **most massive** stars; gravity is so strong that **not even light can escape**.
Larger mass of the remaining core, stronger gravity, more extreme end.
Both are formed because **gravity overcomes** every outward pressure once fusion has stopped.

callouts.p: An extremely dense remnant of a supernova, made mainly of neutrons.
A remnant of a very massive star where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape.

core.p: Exam questions often give you a list of stages and ask you to put them in order, or to say which stages only happen to massive stars. Learn this table.
bullets: Stages shared by **both**: nebula, main sequence star.
Only for **Sun-like** stars: red giant, white dwarf.
Only for **massive** stars: red supergiant, supernova, neutron star, black hole.
Massive stars **live shorter lives** despite having more fuel, because they fuse it much faster.

callouts.p: Write the sequence in full with arrows. A missing or wrongly ordered stage usually loses the mark.

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain each change in terms of the balance between thermal expansion and gravity, not just name the stages.
bullets: Nebula: **gravity** pulls dust and gas together; nothing yet resists it, so it **collapses and heats up**.
Main sequence: fusion starts; **thermal expansion balances gravity**, so the star is **stable**.
Red giant or supergiant: core hydrogen runs out, core contracts and heats; new fusion releases more energy, so **thermal expansion pushes the outer layers out**.
White dwarf: fusion ends; **gravity** compresses the core into a small, dense star.
Supernova: fusion ends in a massive core; **gravity** causes a **sudden collapse**, then an explosion.
Neutron star or black hole: **gravity** compresses the remaining core to extreme density.

callouts.p: Describe means give the stages in order. Explain means also give the reason, usually gravity versus thermal expansion.

analogy.t: A hot-air balloon squeezed by a giant hand
analogy.p: Imagine a hot-air balloon gripped by a giant hand. The hand squeezing inwards is gravity; the burner heating the air so it pushes outwards is fusion causing thermal expansion. With the burner on steadily and the hand squeezing steadily, the balloon stays the same size: a main sequence star. Turn the burner up and the balloon swells: a red giant. Turn the burner off and the hand crushes the balloon: a white dwarf, or for a much stronger hand (more mass) a sudden collapse and explosion like a supernova. Where it breaks down: a star has no fabric skin, its gravity comes from its own mass rather than an outside hand, and the energy comes from nuclear fusion of the star's own fuel, not a burner.

terms.d: A cloud of dust and gas (mainly hydrogen) in space where stars form.
The hot, dense, collapsing ball of gas that forms from a nebula before fusion starts.
The joining of light nuclei (such as hydrogen) to form a heavier nucleus (such as helium), releasing energy.
A stable star fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, with thermal expansion balancing gravity.
The attractive force between masses that pulls a star's matter inwards.
The outward pressure of hot gas, caused by energy released by fusion, which resists gravity.
The state in which the outward effect of thermal expansion equals the inward pull of gravity, so the star is stable.
A large, cool-surfaced red star formed when a Sun-like star runs out of hydrogen in its core and its outer layers expand.
The small, hot, very dense core left after a Sun-like star loses its outer layers; no fusion takes place.
A very large red star formed when a star much more massive than the Sun runs out of core hydrogen.
The huge explosion of a massive star when its core collapses at the end of its life.
An extremely dense supernova remnant made mainly of neutrons.
A remnant of a very massive star whose gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.
The sequence of stages a star passes through from formation to its final remnant, determined by its mass.

mistakes.w: The Sun will end as a supernova or a black hole.
mistakes.r: The Sun has too little mass: it will become a red giant and then a white dwarf.

mistakes.w: A main sequence star is stable because it is not doing anything.
mistakes.r: It is stable because the outward force from thermal expansion (from fusion energy) balances the inward force of gravity.

mistakes.w: Stars burn hydrogen like a fire.
mistakes.r: Hydrogen nuclei undergo nuclear fusion to form helium, releasing energy; it is not combustion.

mistakes.w: A red giant is red because it is hotter.
mistakes.r: A red giant's outer layers have expanded and cooled, so the surface is cooler and looks red.

mistakes.w: More massive stars live longer because they have more fuel.
mistakes.r: More massive stars have stronger gravity, hotter cores and faster fusion, so they have shorter lives.

mistakes.w: A white dwarf is produced by a supernova.
mistakes.r: A white dwarf is the core left by a Sun-like star after its red giant stage; supernovae leave neutron stars or black holes.

mistakes.w: The order is nebula, red giant, main sequence, white dwarf.
mistakes.r: The correct order is nebula, main sequence star, red giant, white dwarf.

mistakes.w: When fusion stops the star explodes outwards because of pressure.
mistakes.r: When fusion stops there is no outward thermal expansion, so gravity makes the core collapse; for massive stars this collapse leads to a supernova.

mistakes.w: Black holes form from all stars when they die.
mistakes.r: Only stars much more massive than the Sun can form black holes (or neutron stars) after a supernova.

exam.q: State what a nebula is made of.
model: Dust and gas (mainly hydrogen).
exam.tip: Dust and gas is the standard answer.

exam.q: Name the final stage in the life cycle of a star of similar mass to the Sun.
model: White dwarf.
exam.tip: Do not confuse with neutron star or black hole.

exam.q: Give the stages in the life cycle of a star of similar mass to the Sun, in order.
model: Nebula, main sequence star
red giant, white dwarf (all in correct order).
exam.tip: All four stages in the correct order are needed for both marks.

exam.q: Name the process that releases energy in a main sequence star and state what is formed.
model: Nuclear fusion
of hydrogen (nuclei) to form helium.
exam.tip: Say fusion, not burning or fission.

exam.q: Explain why a main sequence star is stable.
model: The outward force from thermal expansion (due to energy from fusion)
balances the inward force of gravity.
exam.tip: Name both effects and their directions, and say they are balanced.

exam.q: Explain how a star forms from a nebula.
model: Gravity pulls the dust and gas together
the material becomes denser and hotter as it collapses
when hot/dense enough, nuclear fusion of hydrogen begins and a (main sequence) star forms.
exam.tip: Gravity, collapse and heating, then fusion: three marks.

exam.q: Explain why a star like the Sun becomes a red giant.
model: Hydrogen in the core runs out
the core contracts and heats up, so helium (and shell hydrogen) fusion releases more energy
thermal expansion is greater than gravity so the outer layers expand (and cool, so the star looks red).
exam.tip: Link each step with so or because.

exam.q: Describe the evolution of a star with a mass much larger than the Sun after it leaves the main sequence.
model: It becomes a red supergiant
it then explodes as a supernova
leaving a neutron star
or, if very massive, a black hole.
exam.tip: Neutron star OR black hole depending on mass: mention both outcomes.

exam.q: A student says that massive stars should live longer than the Sun because they have more hydrogen. Evaluate this statement.
model: Massive stars do have more hydrogen
but stronger gravity makes the core hotter and denser, so fusion is much faster
so they use up their fuel more quickly and have shorter lives; the statement is wrong.
exam.tip: Evaluate means agree with the correct part, then explain why the conclusion is wrong.

exam.q: Explain how the balance between thermal expansion and gravity affects the life cycle of stars of similar mass to the Sun and of stars much more massive than the Sun.
model: Nebula: gravity pulls dust and gas together, which heats up until fusion starts
main sequence: thermal expansion from fusion energy balances gravity, so the star is stable
when core hydrogen runs out, the core contracts and heats; more fusion makes thermal expansion greater, so the outer layers expand into a red giant (Sun-like) or red supergiant (massive)
Sun-like star: fusion stops, outer layers lost, gravity compresses the core into a white dwarf
massive star: fusion stops, gravity causes the core to collapse suddenly, producing a supernova
the remnant is a neutron star or, for the most massive stars, a black hole, because gravity is so strong.
exam.tip: Level 3: both life cycles in order, with each change explained by whether gravity or thermal expansion is greater.

worked.q: Model answer: explain what happens to a star like the Sun once it can no longer carry out fusion.
steps: At the end of the red giant stage the star runs out of fuel it can fuse.
The outer layers drift away into space.
With no fusion, there is no energy to cause outward thermal expansion.
Gravity is now greater, so the remaining core contracts.
It becomes a small, very hot, very dense white dwarf, which slowly cools.
worked.ans: The outer layers are lost and gravity compresses the core into a white dwarf, which gradually cools as no fusion takes place.

worked.q: Applied example: Star A has 1 solar mass and Star B has 20 solar masses. Compare their life cycles.
steps: Both form from a nebula and become main sequence stars fusing hydrogen into helium.
Star B has much stronger gravity, so a hotter, denser core and faster fusion, so a shorter main sequence life.
When core hydrogen runs out, Star A becomes a red giant; Star B becomes a red supergiant.
Star A then loses its outer layers and becomes a white dwarf.
Star B explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole.
worked.ans: Star A: nebula, main sequence, red giant, white dwarf (long life). Star B: nebula, main sequence (short), red supergiant, supernova, neutron star or black hole.

worked.q: Model answer: a sequencing question gives the stages supernova, nebula, red supergiant, black hole, main sequence star. Put them in order and state the type of star.
steps: Every star starts as a nebula.
Fusion of hydrogen begins: main sequence star.
Supernova and black hole only happen to stars much more massive than the Sun, so the next stage is red supergiant, not red giant.
The red supergiant explodes as a supernova.
The most massive cores collapse to a black hole.
worked.ans: Nebula, main sequence star, red supergiant, supernova, black hole: the life cycle of a star much more massive than the Sun.
